articles.title_zh: Artisan Cotton Candy Back At EPCOT’s China Pavilion
articles.content_orig:
A post shared by World of Walt (@worldofwaltcom)
Artisan cotton candy shaped like butterflies and Christmas trees is back at EPCOT’s China Pavilion. Prices run from $14 to $25 depending on the design.
This isn’t your average fair cotton candy – it’s more of a sculpted souvenir than a snack. Worth a look if you’re wandering through China Pavilion anyway and want something photogenic to carry around World Showcase.

articles.title_orig: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation
articles.title_zh: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation
articles.content_orig:
Arrests made after three properties were searched in relation to inquiry into late businessman
French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris , in relation to an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking by Mohamed Al Fayed.
Several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released, according to the Paris public prosecutor’s office. Another property in Paris and one in Saint-Tropez, both with links to Fayed, were also searched in mid-October.
Several of Fayed’s alleged victims were also interviewed by officers from the organised crime division of the Paris prosecutor’s office.
It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into “allegations of human trafficking committed by an organised group, aggravated pimping committed by an organised group, and rape”.
In an email sent to survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse earlier today, the Metropolitan police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in a coordinated operation with French investigators.
The Paris prosecutor’s office said: “Searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed , and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.”
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed, it added.
One of the properties that was raided was Castel Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez is one of the most exclusive villas on the French Riviera, and where Diana, Princess of Wales , stayed with her sons in the summer of 1997, at the start of her relationship with Fayed’s son, Dodi.
The other was Villa Windsor , a former holiday home of the Fayed family. The property in western Paris was previously the family home of Charles de Gaulle, before he was president of France, and King Edward VIII, after his abdication, and his wife, Wallis Simpson.
A Met spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France last month and were present during the operation.
Campaign groups representing Fayed’s alleged victims called on the Met police to conduct its own searches of the late billionaire’s properties.
Co-chairs of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, said: “We want to see the same thoroughness applied to every property where survivors say they were taken or abused, including here in Britain. The searches in Paris and Saint-Tropez must be the beginning, not the end.”
A spokesperson for No One Above , a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said: “The French authorities have put this in the hands of their specialist trafficking unit and their organised crime prosecutors, and are investigating it as trafficking by an organised gang.
“The evidence in this case was never confined to Harrods. For two years, the Met has avoided treating it as what France recognised from the outset: organised trafficking by a network. The National Crime Agency should now take over the investigation.”
Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she was overjoyed by the French police raids. “Survivors deserve actions, not words,” she added.
Last November, she told French investigators from the Central Office for the Repression of Human Trafficking that Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris , had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of € 65,000 a year if she slept with him.
Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 169 victims who have contacted the force directly.
The Ritz Paris told Agence France-Presse news agency that it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour” and that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”.

articles.title_orig: Canada’s Carney to raise election meddling concerns in talks with China’s Xi
articles.title_zh: Canada’s Carney to raise election meddling concerns in talks with China’s Xi
articles.content_orig:
A recent public inquiry identified China as ‘the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions’
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that he would stress the importance of “non-interference in our affairs by China” when he meets President Xi Jinping later this month.
A 2025 public inquiry into allegations of election meddling identified China as “the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions”.
Carney confirmed he would meet Xi at the November 18-19 Apec summit and would discuss “many things”, including efforts to broaden bilateral trade.

articles.title_orig: Trump was told on China trip in May about Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy: NYT
articles.title_zh: Trump was told on China trip in May about Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy: NYT
articles.content_orig:
Following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission on Sunday to an extramarital affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, the chipmaker's relationship to China is about to come under intense scrutiny in Washington, D.C.
Since October 2022, when the Biden administration announced sweeping controls to limit China's ability to obtain advanced U.S. chips, Nvidia has seen its business diminish in the world's second-largest economy. Months after an even stricter set of rules was implemented by the Trump administration, Huang said in October 2025, "We are 100% out of China."
The recent allegations against Huang, while throwing the chipmaker into crisis, have also brought attention to the Nvidia CEO's potential influence over U.S. policy on chip sales to China, where its business once flourished. Of particular interest is whether restricted Nvidia chips have reached Chinese companies through customers like Singapore-based Megaspeed , the company linked to Alice Huang.
The New York Times first reported that the Chinese businesswoman was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to people briefed on the intelligence circulated in a memo among the Trump administration in the spring. China has called the allegation a smear.
Jensen Huang has been closely aligned with President Donald Trump during his second administration, helping advise the White House on artificial intelligence safety regulations, while also pushing for looser restrictions on selling AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia would be allowed to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. In March, Huang told reporters that Nvidia had "received purchase orders, and we're in the process of restarting our manufacturing ."
Huang was a last-minute addition to the roster of tech executives who joined Trump on a trip to China in May, after the president was briefed on intelligence concerns, according to the Times .
"In 35 years, I haven't seen a chip CEO with this much direct influence on export policy," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO at Moor Insights & Strategy, in an email.
Since last week's midterm elections that included sweeping victories across the country for Democrats, the mood in Washington has changed. Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed.
Democratic lawmakers, who are about to take power in the House and Senate, have said publicly that Congress will investigate and seek answers. Trump said Monday that he was "amazed" by the allegations and that Huang told him he "had no idea that she was a spy." The FBI is now looking into the issue, Trump said at a White House briefing.
It's been a long four years for Nvidia in China.
Before the initial export controls in 2022, China made up nearly a quarter of Nvidia's revenue. Nvidia responded to the Biden-era restrictions by redesigning some of its products to comply with the new regulations.
"It was a turbulent month or so as the company went upside down to re-engineer" the products, Huang told CNBC in a 2023 interview. Still, he was confident the company could continue selling chips to China. "I think we're going to be just fine in the ability to serve the customers there," he said.
After the Biden administration tightened export restrictions again, Nvidia redesigned another AI graphics processing unit for China, the H20. Following reports that Chinese model developer DeepSeek was using restricted Nvidia chips, the Trump administration limited sales of H20. Nvidia revealed it would incur $5.5 billion in costs related to canceled orders for the redesigned chip.
However, despite saying in its forecasts that "we're assuming 0% for China," the company maintained business in the region. In the last fiscal year, Nvidia reported that about 9% of its revenue came from China, including Hong Kong, although that includes revenue from segments outside of restricted data center chips, such as gaming, auto and industrial. Nvidia's China revenue was 8% in the most recent quarter.
A report in May from short seller Culper Research alleged Nvidia's China exposure was much higher. The firm said that more than 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by China, supported by "illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries," according to the report.
A loophole allows Chinese companies to rent Nvidia GPUs in data centers, even when they're restricted from buying them outright. For example, a Chinese company could lease Nvidia computing power in Europe by renting server capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that's exempt from export controls.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment for this story.
Megaspeed , an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, has been accused of diverting its own supply of Nvidia's restricted AI chips to Chinese companies. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and said inspections found no evidence of violations.
In 2025, Nvidia changed the way it reported regional sales to categorize by customer headquarters, instead of by where the products were billed. Nvidia also stopped reporting Singapore sales during the same period.
"Whether Blackwell chips reached China is a Megaspeed question that predates this week," said Moorhead, pointing to Bloomberg reporting in December 2025 that found Megaspeed had imported 50,000 more Nvidia chips than Nvidia tallied in its data centers.
In 2025, a House Select Committee opened an investigation into whether China's DeepSeek operates on Nvidia's chips.
A separate investigation by the U.S. Commerce Department was centered on Megaspeed. That probe was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department, the Times reported , following an email from Nvidia's general counsel to the Commerce Department seeking information about the investigation.
The restrictions aren't just coming from the U.S. China has continued to limit the amount of Nvidia chips it will allow into the country, keeping Nvidia's China sales numbers down. The U.S. has licensed H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, but Beijing hasn't approved large-scale imports, Moorhead told CNBC. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
Moorhead expects more export control legislation to pass as a result of the latest turmoil. Proposals could allow Congress oversight of chip export licenses or require chipmakers to install security mechanisms to track the location of chips to determine if they've found their way to China.
"Every China license now gets read through this story," Moorhead said. "Jensen has been Nvidia's lead voice on China, and that voice is weaker."
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Seema Mody contributed reporting to this report.
Correction: Three House committees have requested closed-door briefings with the Nvidia CEO about his relationship with Megaspeed. An earlier version misstated the time element.

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine begin U.S.-backed peace talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine begin U.S.-backed peace talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the US will reconvene for a second day of talks on Wednesday
The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.
While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".
Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".
Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.
Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.
At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".
Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.
Until now European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.
The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".
However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.
Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.
Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.
A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are part of the US delegation that will attend the talks in Abu Dhabi
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
From the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump â who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day â has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine that "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result in a fair peace.
Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Russia's Vladimir Putin start real negotiations was by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.
"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi includes Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.
Kyiv has sent several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.
Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof that Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations".
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

articles.title_orig: Singapore seizes US-operated cruise ship that offered ‘permanent’ life at sea
articles.title_zh: Singapore seizes US-operated cruise ship that offered ‘permanent’ life at sea
articles.content_orig:
MV Odyssey impounded by authorities almost a fortnight after passengers left stranded in Cambodian port
Singapore has seized a US-operated cruise ship that offered retirees a “permanent” life at sea but instead offloaded them in Cambodia after it ran out of money due to soaring fuel prices.
After more than 200 passengers were left stranded in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville last month , the MV Odyssey sailed on to ⁠Singapore last week and has been impounded by authorities.
“The vessel has been placed under arrest ⁠pursuant to a court order,” Singapore’s Maritime and Port ​Authority said in ‌a statement. “The crew onboard ‌are reported to be well and arrangements for their ‌welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel’s creditors. There are no passengers on board.”
According to court records , ​the MV Odyssey was listed “under sheriff’s arrest” on Sunday morning ​just off Singapore’s east coast, meaning it had been detained but was not necessarily under any criminal charges.
It was not clear why the ship had been impounded, although Singapore is a global shipping hub, and it is not unusual for ships facing commercial issues to relocate to the city-state to resolve disputes.
The local Straits Times reported that the ship’s Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, owed approximately US$500,000 in fuel payments . Villa Vie Residences has been contacted for comment.
On 27 October, and with only a few hours’ notice, the company disembarked all passengers , saying fuel ⁠price surges from the Iran war had made operations ​“unsustainable”. Mikael Petterson, the founder ‌and executive chair of Villa Vie Residences, later said the ship was now being operated by creditors.
Most of the passengers of the MV Odyssey were Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials said.
Passengers were sold what the company website said was “a new model of global living at sea”, with the 195-metre (640-ft) vessel offering multi-year residencies as well as permanent cabin costs between $120,000 (£90,000) and $440,000. However, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, the company said in a statement.
Some passengers have stayed in Cambodia to assess their options, including Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube. In a video published last week and filmed on a beach with the Odyssey in the background, the couple said the “bank” was now making a decision on its fate. They later filmed the ship leaving at night.
The round-the-world cruise faced issues from the start, including a four-month delay in setting sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024. Several passengers reported signs of financial distress during the cruise, including accounts of guests raising extra money for fuel.
Randy Cassingham, a writer living onboard the ship, said after passengers were off-loaded, residents had also passed a jar around to raise $100 each for lower-ranking crew. He said few passengers expected to recover any of the funds they had spent on their cabins, as they knew the company had “been in terrible money problems from the beginning”.

articles.title_orig: PS Plus Pulls Plug on PC Streaming After Fewer Than 1% Used It
articles.title_zh: PS Plus Pulls Plug on PC Streaming After Fewer Than 1% Used It
articles.content_orig:
Sony will kill the ability to stream PlayStation games on the PC beginning 10th December, with the platform holder stating fewer than 0.4% of eligible PS Plus Premium subscribers used it.
Members of the manufacturer’s most expensive tier can currently stream and play titles from the PS Plus Premium catalogue using a PC app, which will be discontinued next month.
Curiously, this service has always been limited to PS4 and PS3 titles – it never expanded support to the PS5 library.
The pages on PlayStation.com where you used to be able to download the software have already been removed in anticipation.
Writing on the PS Blog , Sony’s Adam Michel said:
“PlayStation believes in providing high-quality experiences to our players, and we regularly review offerings to ensure we are focusing on experiences our members value most. With a very small number of eligible PS Plus Premium members (less than 0.4%) using the PS Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use. As a result, the PS Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available.”
Once upon a time, I did temporarily use PS Now streaming on my laptop when I went through a period where I didn’t have access to my consoles. But I haven’t used the feature since.
I don’t think Sony promoted this particularly prominently, so I expect many fans may only be finding out about it now.
But I think this is probably part of a broader push by the Japanese giant to move its software off PC. Internally, it’s pivoted away from porting its first-party single player games to the platform. Now it’s ceasing streaming as well.
It should be stressed that PS Plus Premium cloud streaming will remain available on the PS5, PS4, and PS Portal. There will also be no changes to Remote Play functionality.
Will you be affected by this at all? Given the numbers touted in Sony’s article, I can’t imagine many of you will have used this.

articles.title_orig: In Argentina, Pope Leo Walks in the Giant Shadow of Francis
articles.title_zh: In Argentina, Pope Leo Walks in the Giant Shadow of Francis
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV met with bishops, priests, deacons, religious, seminarians and pastoral workers at the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption in Córdoba on Tuesday, the third day of his apostolic visit to Argentina.
The encounter included a welcome address by Cardinal Ángel Sixto Rossi, in which he called for a Church attentive to peopleâs needs, particularly those most wounded, and committed to walking alongside them in neighbourhoods, prisons and hospitals, as well as testimonies from four people involved in the life of the Church.
In his address, the Pope invited those present to return to the source of their vocation and renew their relationship with Christ, recalling the spiritual tradition of Argentina and figures such as Mama Antula, Saint José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero and Pope Francis.
Drawing on the Ignatian Spiritual Exercises, he asked them to consider the question: âWhy are we here?â He warned that pastoral commitments can sometimes take the place of prayer and intimacy with God.
âWe work hard for God yet spend less and less time with him,â he said, calling for renewed attention to the Eucharist, the Word of God and personal prayer.
Pope Leo also highlighted the need for ongoing conversion, humility and freedom to respond to God's call, including when it leads in unexpected directions. He encouraged pastoral workers to examine their lives and remain open to the places and people to whom they are sent.
Reflecting on the Church's social mission, he recognised its commitment to those who suffer, while insisting that material assistance must be accompanied by spiritual care and the proclamation of Christ.
Again, he recalled Pope Francis and his teaching, and he quoted Evangelii Gaudium : âthe worst discrimination which the poor suffer is the lack of spiritual care.â
The Church, the Pope added, is not simply a humanitarian organisation, but is sent to bring Christ to the world.
Addressing seminarians, Pope Leo encouraged them to learn to see others through God's eyes and to allow themselves to be evangelised by the people they encounter. âEven those who have the least can teach us a great deal,â he said, referring to the testimony shared during the meeting.
He also spoke of perseverance when ministry brings weariness or few visible results. âEven amid doubts and weariness, one continues to say with oneâs life: âHere I am,ââ he said.
And recalling Saint Héctor Valdivielso Sáez and Saint Brochero, he explained that physical limitations and difficult circumstances need not bring an end to service.
Responding to the testimonies brought by Laura Sampallo, a consecrated woman, and by Father Martín Carranza, a priest of the Archdiocese of Córdoba, the Pope recalled his own recent hospitalisation and encouraged those present not to lose their missionary zeal.
âOur strength may run out, but Godâs power never will,â he said, adding that technology can also help the Church continue to proclaim the Gospel.
Bringing his address to a close, Pope Leo returned to the Ignatian prayer of offering oneself to God: âTake, Lord, and receiveâ¦â He invited those present to ask whether the Lord could still make use of them. âIf the answer remains âyes,â then there is much ahead of us. Let us not give up!â
Finally, he encouraged the Church in Argentina to continue fostering vocations, vibrant parishes, religious communities and seminaries capable of forming people for holiness. He also recalled Pope Francisâ appeal to young people in Rio de Janeiro, in which he spoke of a Church that continues to âmake noiseâ through its missionary presence.
Pope Leo concluded by entrusting the Church in Argentina to Our Lady of Luján and urging those present to return to their communities with renewed hope, freedom, and commitment to their mission.

articles.title_orig: Despite Denial, Trump Was Told on Trip to China About Spying on Nvidia Leader
articles.title_zh: Despite Denial, Trump Was Told on Trip to China About Spying on Nvidia Leader
articles.content_orig:
The PC revolution was upon us, and American tech companies were running circles around Compagnie des Machines Bull, the legendary but struggling French computer company.
France was determined to find out how and why. Between 1987 and 1989 , the Direction Générale de la Sécurité Extérieure, France’s equivalent of the CIA, planted moles inside the offices of Bull’s biggest American competitors, IBM and Texas Instruments, where the spies passed trade secrets back to the French company. The FBI and CIA ultimately uncovered the scheme and the employees were fired.
Four decades later, the global Big Tech corporate espionage problem has grown – and so have the stakes.
US-based Nvidia, the world’s largest and most important AI chipmaker, is investigating reports that it was a victim of a foreign surveillance effort . CEO Jensen Huang also acknowledged he had an extramarital affair. Although Huang and Nvidia haven’t provided details or connected those two revelations, The New York Times reported last week that the US State Department developed significant scrutiny of Huang’s relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed.
Silicon Valley is particularly vulnerable to corporate espionage: The cutting-edge technologies it develops have grown vital to the global economy, and OpenAI, Google, Apple and many other high-profile tech companies in recent weeks and months have reported foreign and domestic spying attempts at their companies.
“Corporate espionage has always been a big challenge, but today it’s especially so in areas where US firms are building technologies that are foundational to economic, military and other forms of power,” said Matthew Waxman, cybersecurity law professor at Columbia University.
But Big Tech’s spy problem is almost certainly a lot bigger than anyone realizes.
Explore the true stories of America’s covert operations
As IT exploded in economic import over the past several decades, information has become one of the world’s most valuable commodities. That has turned Big Tech’s secrets into the gold sitting in the underground vault – and made it rife for theft.
AI has significantly intensified the battle for trade secrets.
Cyberattacks and digital intrusions aren’t going anywhere. But the higher stakes of acquiring trade secrets have placed a renewed emphasis on human espionage inside corporations, said Greg Pollock, director of research and insights at risk management company UpGuard.
“It’s true that huge amounts of data have been compromised through hacking, but the most important information is still what’s said in private,” Pollock said.
The most sophisticated actors don’t choose only one path to gain access to trade secrets: Cyberattacks can help countries and companies steal information, but a human source can help advise what secrets matter and what decisions will be made about them, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.
Adversaries looking to obtain trade secrets through old-fashioned in-person espionage tend to accomplish that in one of two ways: hiring away employees who are willing to spill the beans or plant moles who befriend people.
Having a human on the inside gives companies a potentially much longer timeframe to obtain information than via cyberattack alone – which tend to trip alarm bells after a while. Humans, by contrast, may be able to access key documents that could be related to their everyday tasks – or at least appear to be, noted Madhu Shashanka, cofounder of security firm Concentric AI.
And, unlike computers, humans can gain the trust of employees, many of whom hold keys to crucial information. That makes anyone a target.
“It’s not just the CEOs who are targeted, and it doesn’t all look like a James Bond movie,” said Krauthamer. “The average Silicon Valley employee knows to be on the lookout for phishing scams. But humans trust other humans. That’s just a growing risk.”
That risk long predates the computer era.
Corporate espionage dates back to at least 1700, when French Jesuit priest François Xavier d’Entrecolles was sent on a mission to Jingdezhen, China – but not the kind of mission you’re probably thinking of.
Imported Chinese porcelain was flooding the dining rooms of Europe’s elite in the early 18th century, and d’Entrecolles was sent to Jingdezhen, home of the country’s porcelain factories, to determine the manufacturing process that had stumped European porcelain makers. D’Entrecolles, who spoke Chinese, spent the next two decades touring factories and interviewing families to determine the secret behind Chinese porcelain. In 1712, he wrote his first letter to the treasurer of the Jesuits’ China missions with a details of the materials used, as well as the process for purifying, molding and firing the porcelain.
Security experts agree that the corporate espionage problem has grown significantly over the past several hundred years – and particularly in the past decade. But how much it’s expanding can’t be fully known.
US federal courts saw a record 1,500 trade secret cases filed last year. And high-profile cases have been a constant in the news lately. A month before the revelations of Huang’s affair, OpenAI said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” in one of its US offices planted by a Saudi employee who had used an internal productivity tool to determine when and where high-profile executives were meeting. (The former employee pleaded not guilty to the charges.) And in February, the US Justice Department indicted three former Google employees who were spying for foreign countries, including Iran.
But the cases we know about are just scratching the surface of a potentially much more prevalent concern, said Elizabeth Rowe, a University of Virginia law professor specializing in trade secrets and intellectual property.
“It’s a bigger problem than we are aware of,” said Rowe. “The ways these cases come to our attention tend to undercount how pervasive it is.”
The most recent federal statute that criminalizes this espionage, passed in the late 1990s, relies heavily on companies self-reporting. Companies can also take civil action against adversaries, but that still relies on corporations speaking out.
The problem: Businesses have many incentives not to talk about the problem of corporate espionage.
Companies that go to court signal to investors that they lost potentially crucial information. Civil suits – particularly those dealing with complex trade-secret lawsuits – can be incredibly expensive.
The biggest barrier: Filing a complaint exposes the trade secrets and makes them vulnerable to being lost through the lawsuit or the press.
“All this suggests when you see a case that makes headlines, there are many, many more that never made it to the public,” said Rowe.

articles.title_orig: China Lifts The Veil On Its GJ-11 Mysterious Dragon Stealth UCAV
articles.title_zh: China Lifts The Veil On Its GJ-11 Mysterious Dragon Stealth UCAV
articles.content_orig:
China has provided us with the clearest look yet at its GJ-11 stealth uncrewed combat aerial vehicle (UCAV), with new official footage revealing previously unseen details of the flying-wing drone, including its internal weapons bays, landing gear, nose-mounted sensor installation, and distinctive exhaust arrangement.
The release also comes alongside a claim from the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) that the GJ-11 has completed its first live-fire strike mission, scoring a hit. This is somewhat puzzling, since the UCAV has racked up test sorties for years already, including at forward operating locations, and it seems almost inconceivable that a live weapons delivery would not have been conducted before now. Perhaps this is a case of something being lost in translation, such as the use of a new internal sensor or a new type of weapon delivery.
The footage, broadcast by Chinese state television’s CCTV yesterday, comes two days ahead of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the PLAAF. Accompanying reporting provides additional details about the aircraft’s intended mission set, including airstrikes and suppression of enemy air defenses (SEAD), as well as its integration into manned-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) operations with crewed fighters.
The new disclosures offer the most comprehensive public look yet at the GJ-11’s configuration and provide further insight into how China intends to employ the stealthy flying-wing aircraft, which is named Xuanlong — Chinese for Mystery Dragon.
One of the most revealing views shows the underside of the GJ-11, clearly exposing its two internal weapons bays. Located within the aircraft’s blended wing-body, the ventral bays have separate sets of doors with distinctive serrated edges — a common feature on low-observable aircraft. The internal arrangement and dimensions of the bays remain unclear, as does the precise range of weapons the aircraft can accommodate. However, it would appear likely that each bay can accommodate at least a 1,000-pound-class and likely a 2,000-pound-class weapon.
#GTMilitaryWatch CCTV News military channel released new footage on Monday offering a close-up, multi-angle look at the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force's GJ-11 stealth drone. It also revealed that two of the Air Force's first batch of self-trained female drone… pic.twitter.com/PPVmws9DJJ
According to CCTV , the two bays can carry a variety of air-to-ground/surface munitions. The weapons bay configuration had previously been revealed in a model of the GJ-11 displayed by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) at Airshow China in 2021, but the new footage provides a much better look at the actual aircraft.
Internal weapons carriage is central to the GJ-11’s low-observable design, allowing it to carry munitions without the radar signature (and aerodynamic) penalties associated with external pylons and stores.
Previous footage released in November 2025 showed the GJ-11 in flight with its landing gear remaining extended. However, one of the new sequences shows the aircraft taking off, with subsequent side and rear views capturing its landing gear retracting after liftoff. The landing gear itself is notably robust, including a heavy-duty twin-wheel nose unit. With that in mind, it may be the same landing gear as used in the GJ-21, a naval variant capable of operating from aircraft carriers and big-deck assault ships.
The new imagery also offers a closer look at a trapezoidal glazed fairing beneath the nose. This appears consistent with an electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensor installation. Its precise configuration and capabilities have not been disclosed, but it’s worth noting that similar-looking installations also appear on the crewed J-20 and J-35 fighters, with these systems apparently being analogous to the electro-optical targeting system, or EOTS, found on the F-35 . If the sensor on the GJ-11 works like an EOTS, it would provide the drone with precision targeting and identification, lasing, as well as a secondary infrared search-and-track emulation function.
Perhaps the most distinctive external feature remains the GJ-11’s exhaust arrangement, for what is reported to be a WS-13 turbofan engine. A close-up of the rear of the aircraft shows the flattened exhaust outlet, shielded and integrated into the upper rear portion of the flying-wing airframe. Combined with the dorsal air intake and the absence of conventional exposed engine nozzles, this configuration is intended to reduce the aircraft’s radar and infrared signatures, especially from the most critical view aspects. The GJ-11’s tailless, blended-wing configuration is by now a defining feature of low-observable UCAV designs.
At least some of the GJ-11s shown have an air data boom on the nose. While normally associated with early flight testing, the GJ-11 is now far beyond that. The booms could still be fitted for some envelope expansion and other flight test work, although it may also simply involve earlier footage.
Beyond the new imagery, one of the more interesting aspects of the CCTV coverage is its description of the GJ-11’s intended operational role.
The broadcaster identified airstrikes and SEAD among the aircraft’s mission sets. The latter is particularly significant, as penetrating or operating within heavily defended airspace to locate and suppress or destroy enemy air defense systems is the most dangerous mission for a crewed combat aircraft.
A stealthy uncrewed aircraft could contribute to these operations by carrying precision-guided weapons into more contested areas, providing additional sensing and targeting capacity, or forcing an adversary to expend valuable air defense resources.
The two internal weapons bays provide the means to carry air-to-surface munitions while retaining the aircraft’s low-observable configuration. However, we don’t know which specific weapons have been integrated, their quantities, or whether the GJ-11 can employ dedicated anti-radiation weapons for SEAD missions. Alternative SEAD/DEAD loads could include multiple Small Diameter Bomb (SDB) equivalents, including those that are networked, as we have seen in previous concept videos . Many other types of standoff weapons could also be carried, with the platform itself using onboard sensors for fixing the target or acquiring targeting information from other sources via a tactical data network.
According to CCTV , the GJ-11 has completed its first live-fire strike mission, with two members of the PLAAF’s initial batch of female drone operators participating in the operation.
One of the operators, Shi Xiaoran, described encountering cloud cover that initially obscured the target. After circling once more, she located it and released the weapon, scoring a hit.
One aspect that remains unclear is the extent to which the aircraft can independently identify and engage targets. A successful strike would demonstrate weapons employment, but not necessarily autonomous targeting or engagement.
Perhaps the most strategically important aspect of the new coverage is its emphasis on manned-unmanned teaming.
The CCTV footage showed mission planning involving a GJ-11 operating alongside J-16 Flanker multirole fighters and, in a separate sequence, J-20 fifth-generation stealth fighters.
This provides a more explicit indication of the role China envisions for the GJ-11 within its broader combat aviation ecosystem.
The J-16 provides a powerful multirole platform for strike and electronic warfare-related missions , while the J-20 offers a stealthy crewed counterpart for operations in highly contested airspace. An uncrewed aircraft operating alongside either type could extend the formation’s sensor coverage, carry additional weapons, conduct reconnaissance, or undertake particularly hazardous missions.

articles.title_orig: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
articles.title_zh: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
articles.content_orig:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
after newsletter promotion
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

articles.title_orig: IBM to End Immigration Sponsorship for Roles in Biggest Unit
articles.title_zh: IBM to End Immigration Sponsorship for Roles in Biggest Unit
articles.content_orig:
IBM said it's ending immigration sponsorships for "a majority of roles" in its biggest unit.
"IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages," an IBM spokesperson said in a statement. "That participation has been declining for a number of years and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting."
The news, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes as the Trump administration has sought to crack down on tech companies' reliance on foreign workers. In September 2025, President Donald Trump introduced a $100,000 fee on some H-1 B applicants, though that proposal is tied up in the courts.
Last month, Vice President JD Vance announced that the Trump administration was suspending Microsoft from a federal program that companies use to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency. Vance said that the tech company had abused the Permanent Labor Certification process, often called PERM.
IBM Consulting is by far the largest unit of the tech giant. According to its website, there are over 150,000 consultants. In its 2025 annual report, IBM reported having 264,300 employees across IBM and its wholly owned subsidiaries.
According to federal records, IBM had just over 1,600 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal year 2026, compared to over 2,000 in FY 2025 and nearly 3,000 in FY 2024. The records are for IBM as a whole, meaning they alone wouldn't determine how many IBM Consulting employees are being sponsored. The figures may also not represent new workers, as they can refer to amended or extended applications for existing employees.
Bloomberg reported that employees affected by the change can continue working for IBM outside the US or leave the company by the end of the year.

articles.title_orig: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.title_zh: Chip stocks' slide nears $5 trillion as Nvidia hits most extreme selling level since 2019
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It took five minutes for Tuesday's hot inflation report to knock stocks lower, and chip stocks struggled to hold an early rebound. Nvidia ( NVDA ) hasn't been sold this hard, this fast since 2019, but the typical S&P 500 stock is barely down.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was down nearly 1% midday Tuesday, shedding about $500 billion in market value according to Yahoo Finance calculations, while the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell more than 1%. The equal-weighted S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ), which gives every company the same weight, was down only about 0.2%.
Nvidia fell about 6%, slicing through the $170 level chart watchers flagged, and is on track for its lowest close since March 30 as the scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang drags on. Its relative strength index , a gauge of how fast and how hard a stock has moved, sank to 23 out of a possible 100 — its most oversold reading since June 2019.
Read more: Nvidia stock drops as spy fiasco involving CEO Jensen Huang raises broader risk concerns
Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SanDisk ( SNDK ) and chip designer Arm ( ARM ) fell roughly 3% to 5%. AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) held up after Monday's surge.
The longer view is starker. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks has lost about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, roughly a quarter of its worth. That's more than the roughly $3 trillion the entire S&P 500 has shed over the same stretch, even though the basket includes some companies outside the index.
Tuesday's trigger was a hotter-than-expected October Consumer Price Index . S&P 500 futures fell about 0.5% in the five minutes after the 8:30 a.m. ET release, on volume many times the morning's norm. Nasdaq-100 futures briefly erased their losses by 10 a.m., then slid again.
Bonds felt it too. The 5-year Treasury yield ( ^FVX ) was on track for its biggest one-day jump since April 2025, and the 10-year ( ^TNX ) climbed back above 5% as traders raised bets on a December rate hike .
BofA's Savita Subramanian sees the bigger risk in the S&P 500 itself.
"We're not particularly bullish on the index. I think the index itself is a bit risky," the head of US equity and quantitative strategy at BofA Securities told Yahoo Finance on Tuesday. "What's the most crowded equity ticker in the world? It's the S&P index."
The typical stock looks nothing like the index. The equal-weighted S&P 500 is up about 4% since Oct. 6 and closed at a record on Nov. 4.
Some see Nvidia's slide as a chance to buy. "I think if [CEO Jensen Huang] stays, then this is going to prove to be overdone. And you know this will be a strong buying opportunity," Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon said Monday on Yahoo Finance's "Deirdre Bosa Live."
Veteran trader Michael Martin isn't convinced . "I don't think these are buying opportunities. Everything is in a downtrend," he told Yahoo Finance on Friday.
The Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) turned lower Monday right at its 200-day moving average , and the Cboe Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) is holding above 20, a level associated with expectations of higher-than-average volatility over the next month.
Nvidia reports quarterly results after the bell on Nov. 17, and Anthropic's IPO could follow as soon as Nov. 19.
Subramanian isn't giving up on the AI trade. "I think you want to stay long," she said. "The idea that AI is not the metaverse. It's going to continue."
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.

articles.content_orig:
Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.
The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.
It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.
Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details:
Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf
As the post notes, here’s what the app does:
Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.
And here are the feature highlights:
Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

articles.title_orig: Weil partners approve plan to shut down law firm
articles.title_zh: Weil partners approve plan to shut down law firm
articles.content_orig:
Join 350,000+ subscribers and keep yourself informed with a selection of
The Week’s most interesting, enlightening and entertaining stories - plus daily puzzles.
Your newsletter sign-up was successful
Want to add more newsletters?
The swift downfall of “one of Wall Street’s most vaunted law firms” last week has put the legal industry on edge, said Erin Mulvaney and Andrew Scurria in The Wall Street Journal . Weil, Gotshal & Manges—a fixture among corporate dealmakers for nearly a century—was “one of the 20 most profitable in the business,” raking in $2.1 billion in revenue last year with “relatively few liabilities,” apart from a lease on a roughly 380,000-square-foot office on Fifth Avenue in New York City. What it didn’t have was loyalty. The firm has “hemorrhaged top lawyers” in recent months after rivals poached top partners, including private-equity attorney Ramona Nee, who was chosen to lead the firm in 2027. In September, Weil’s “top dealmaker,” Michael Aiello, left too, and “confidence in Weil’s future cratered” in a matter of weeks. “A law firm’s most valuable asset is its people,” said bankruptcy attorney Albert Togut. “If they go home one night and don’t come back the next day, it’s over.”
This is the “logical consequence of an industry engaging in a Darwinian war for talent,” said Chris Bryant in Bloomberg . Some legal superstars today are making up to $40 million a year, an impossible figure for most small or even midsize firms to match. “Big Law has moved away from paying counsel according to seniority”—which incentivized allegiance—“and has oriented more toward an individual’s results.” It’s created an “eat-what-you-kill” attitude that has made the entire legal industry unstable. Rivals “shouldn’t kid themselves” if they think “the same couldn’t happen to them.”
It also didn’t help that Weil “botched” its succession plan, said Diane Brady in Fortune . The choice of Nee was made unconventionally, without much partner input, and “there was no plan B” when she announced in September that she “no longer planned to take the role.” That’s one of the “lessons” that other CEOs should heed from this “sad narrative.”

The legal industry looks strong today on the surface, said Sara Randazzo in Reuters , but it is “astonishingly fragile.” Unlike corporate executives , partners aren’t “sitting on stock options that give them a powerful financial incentive to stay.” Even a slight “loss of confidence in a firm’s direction can be enough to set off a rush for the exits.”
The partnership structure, “once an instrument of stability, is now a liability” when your talent prefers to think of themselves as “the world’s best-paid gig workers,” said The Economist . How can order be restored? Noncompete agreements have “never been used by law firms” in the U.S., but they are customary in the U.K. and on Wall Street. “The legal industry’s Lehman moment” might require a drastic change to how law firms do business.

articles.content_orig:
Today is Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,235 flaws, including one actively exploited Microsoft Outlook zero-day vulnerability.
This Patch Tuesday addresses 66 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 48 of which are Remote Code Execution (RCE), 15 are Elevation of Privilege (EoP), and three are Use-After-Free in Microsoft Edge.
The approximate number of bugs in each vulnerability category is listed below:
Of the 1,235 vulnerabilities, approximately 639 are categorized under Windows or Microsoft Windows products/components.
When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.
Therefore, today's total excludes 108 flaws fixed earlier this month, including one Entra Device Registration, 82 Mariner, and 25 Microsoft Edge flaws.
November's Patch Tuesday comes after a record-breaking 1,411 flaws in the October updates as Microsoft continues to use AI to find and patch vulnerabilities.
To learn more about the non-security updates released today, you can review our dedicated articles on the Windows 11 KB5132061 & KB5131087 cumulative updates and the Microsoft Windows 10 KB5131096 extended security update .
This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that was exploited in attacks.
Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.
The actively exploited zero-day vulnerability addressed in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates is:
CVE-2026-124194 - Microsoft Outlook Spoofing Vulnerability
Microsoft patched a Microsoft Outlook Spoofing zero-day vulnerability that was actively exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.
"An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook," warns Microsoft.
"Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction."
This type of vulnerability is known as an NTLM credential disclosure flaw, where a malicious attachment, when opened, causes Windows to connect to an attacker-controlled network share.
When connecting, Windows may automatically attempt to authenticate to the remote server, exposing the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash, which can then be captured by the attacker and potentially cracked offline.
The recovered credentials could then be used to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts.
Similar vulnerability have been exploited in the past , typically through malicious attachments sent in phishing campaigns .

articles.title_orig: AIM-174B Long-Range Missile Packed With Glide Munitions Teased, New Details Shared
articles.title_zh: AIM-174B Long-Range Missile Packed With Glide Munitions Teased, New Details Shared
articles.content_orig:
General Atomics says it could shrink its Vektrex howitzer-launched glide munition down to a size small enough for several of them to be packed inside the nose of a missile. The company has already put forward a more specific concept involving an AIM-174B air-to-air missile turned into a strike weapon carrying seven Vektrex-derived submunitions. Being able to load existing and future air- and surface-launched missiles with multiple gliding submunitions could open up new operational possibilities and create additional challenges for defenders.
Naval News was the first to report on the submunition-laden AIM-174B concept after seeing a rendering, seen below, on display at General Atomics’ booth at the Euronaval 2026 exhibition in Paris, France, last week. General Atomics’ Electromagnetic Systems (GA-EMS) division has now provided additional information directly to TWZ .
“We’re exploring a concept for deploying Vektrex-derived maneuvering submunitions from air- and ground-launched missiles to address emerging needs for extended-range precision fires,” Mike Rucker, Vice President of GA-EMS Weapons Programs, told us in a statement. “Our investments in advanced weapons, precision machining, automation and assembly provide a manufacturing foundation to support production as designs qualify and customers commit.”
To take a step back, General Atomics first unveiled Vektrex in 2023, at which time it was called the Long Range Maneuvering Projectile (LRMP). It is an unpowered precision-guided munition with pop-out wings that deploy after launch. Development to date, which has been conducted with support from the U.S. Army and the U.S. Navy , has been focused first on a version of Vektrex that can be fired from standard 155mm howitzers . A concept for a configuration that can be launched via 5-inch naval guns has also been shown.
General Atomics has previously described Vektrex as having “advanced redundant guidance systems” that enable it to hit static or moving targets. The navigation system allows for multiple types of approaches to the target area. In the terminal phase, it can execute a steep dive onto a fixed set of coordinates or follow a differently shaped flight path to that impact point, if desired. It can also switch over to an onboard seeker to find mobile targets. Indirect approach vectors and maneuvering in the latter stages of flight can also improve survivability.
“The underlying artillery application provides the technical starting point [for the submubition concept],” General Atomics’ Rucker told us. “Deployable wings enable aerodynamic glide that multiplies Vektrex’s reach two to three times beyond conventional rounds. Its capabilities include resilient navigation in GPS-degraded or denied environments.”
General Atomics has previously projected the maximum range of a Vektrex round fired from a 155mm howitzer with a 39-caliber barrel to be in excess of 74.5 miles (120 kilometers). The munition’s reach extends further, to more than 124 miles (200), when launched from a longer 52-caliber 155mm howitzer. As a point of comparison, the maximum range of existing U.S. Army 39-caliber 155mm howitzers is generally pegged at around 19 miles when firing unguided rocket-assisted rounds and 25 miles when employing GPS-assisted M982 Excalibur precision-guided shells .
“The missile-carried submunition concept envisions a larger missile carrying and releasing multiple Vektrex-derived maneuvering projectiles,” according to Rucker. “The concept expands the potential delivery options for maneuvering precision payloads, giving prospective customers a concrete configuration to evaluate against their requirements for range, payload, platform compatibility and affordability. Those requirements would guide how we advance the concept.”
“For artillery users, the modernization opportunity is to extend capability while building on existing launcher and support infrastructure. The missile-carried concept explores a different application of that technology,” he added. “While much of the core technology is applicable, this configuration would require additional engineering and validation.”
As noted, General Atomics has already presented one potential pairing in the form of the AIM-174B loaded with seven submunitions. The U.S. Navy officially unveiled the AIM-174B , also known as the Gunslinger, in 2024. It is an air-launched version of the surface-launched Standard Missile-6 (SM-6). The SM-6 is a multi-purpose weapon able to engage a variety of aerial targets, including ballistic missiles and even certain hypersonic threats in the terminal phases of their flight. It can also be employed in a surface-to-surface mode .
The Navy currently describes the AIM-174B as purely an air-to-air missile. However, TWZ has previously highlighted the potential for the Gunslinger to be employed in the air-to-surface mode, especially given its lineage from the SM-6. A version loaded with gliding submunitions could open new options for engaging multiple targets across a broader area, and doing so at extended ranges, just by launching a single missile.
The reach of this particular pairing could be particularly impressive given the surface-launched SM-6’s stated range of well over 200 miles . Unlike the SM-6, which uses a rocket booster for initial launch, the AIM-174 benefits from the altitude and speed of the aircraft firing it. Though not confirmed, Gunslinger’s maximum range by itself can be reasonably understood to be in the hundreds of miles. Vektrex-derived submunitions could easily add dozens of miles of additional range, at least, from their release point.
A version of the AIM-174B in this configuration would enable strikes on targets deeper inside hostile territory while also helping to keep launch platforms away from enemy air defenses. A single missile could also target multiple ships within a surface action group hundreds of miles away. In any scenario, it would also expand the total number of targets a single aircraft could engage on a single sortie.
The full General Atomics rendering showing the submunition-toting Gunslinger also shows it being launched from a F/A-18E/F Super Hornet carrying another one of these missiles. As such, the jet’s loadout would include 14 gliding submunitions on just two stations. A Super Hornet could carry up to four of these missiles, or a total of 28 submunitions. In this case, the fighter is also depicted carrying two Bullseye cruise missiles, two AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles, and two AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missiles. Bullseye is a cooperative development between General Atomics and Israeli defense contractor Rafael.
This is also just one potential combination. Vektrex-derived submunitions capable of being released from an AIM-174B could also be loaded into surface-launched SM-6s. Just within the U.S. military today, there are multiple options for firing SM-6s from ships , as well as from launchers on land .
Based on the AIM-174B concept that has been presented now, there are certainly other suitably large missiles in existence today that could carry various numbers of Vektrex-derived submunitions. The U.S. Army notably has plans already for a future version of its Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) short-range ballistic missile loaded with “enhanced” payloads , which could include precision-guided submunitions and/or drones .
Depending on the cost of the submunitions, General Atomics’ Vektrex-based submunition concept could also offer broader magazine depth and supply chain benefits. The 155mm-howitzer-launched Vektrex is already being designed with an eye toward affordability and producibility.
“Our focus is developing capabilities that help U.S., allied and partner forces extend precision fires, maintain effectiveness when navigation is disrupted, and obtain munitions in the quantities they need,” GA-EMS’ Rucker told us. “Vektrex is one way we are addressing those needs through improvements at the munition level.”
